title: Kolkata ward map fight reaches Supreme Court; Abhishek Banerjee files caveat to be heard
dek: The state wants the top court to lift a High Court bar on calling the Kolkata Municipal Corporation poll on 209 redrawn wards. The Trinamool has asked to be heard before any order is passed.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The fight over Kolkata's new ward map has reached the Supreme Court. The West Bengal government has asked the court to set aside a Calcutta High Court order that stops the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) election being called on the basis of the city's 209 redrawn wards, and Trinamool Congress general secretary Abhishek Banerjee and his party have filed a caveat asking to be heard before any order is passed, according to reports.

A caveat is a request that the court not decide a case without first hearing the person who files it. Mr Banerjee also filed a separate application asking the court to consider the party's submissions, reports said. No date for a hearing had been reported by Tuesday morning.

## What the state is challenging

The state filed its petition on 13 November through advocate Uddyam Mukherjee, the date Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari had set when he said the government would appeal. It challenges an interim order of 6 November by a division bench of Justices Sabyasachi Bhattacharyya and Arjun Ray Mukherjee.

The bench ordered that no election notification be issued under the amended Schedule II of the KMC Act, 1980, which sets out the ward boundaries, until a pending challenge to the delimitation is decided, and restrained the State Election Commission from notifying the poll on the revised boundaries until then, according to reports of the order. It held that the power to recommend ward changes under Section 601 of the Act lies with the elected corporation, not with an administrator appointed after the elected board was dissolved; allowing otherwise, the bench said, would let the state effectively recommend changes to itself. It also held that Article 243ZG of the Constitution, which limits court interference in municipal elections, did not bar the challenge, because the ward map was an executive notification. It said the allegations of malice and gerrymandering needed full adjudication and could not be decided at the interim stage.

## The two sides

The delimitation was challenged by Dipu Das, a CPI(M) councillor from 2005 to 2010, who says the state's notification of 11 September, which raised the number of wards from 144 to 209, was drawn using electoral rolls rather than population figures and was designed to benefit the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party. The Trinamool says the wards were redrawn in a way that helps the BJP and wants the High Court's bar kept in place for now, reports said.

The state has argued in the High Court that it can redraw wards without a recommendation from an elected corporation, that the administrator holds all the corporation's powers while there is no elected board, and that the challenge came too late. Mr Adhikari has dismissed the case, saying earlier this month that "those who are destined to lose the election go to court".

## Background

The KMC, which provides civic services to about 45 lakh people, has had no elected board since June. The single judge hearing the main petition, Justice Hiranmay Bhattacharya, has given the state three weeks to file its affidavit and the petitioner one week after that to reply, and the matter may come up again around 30 November, reports said. Polls to Howrah and five other civic bodies were expected to be held in the same phase as Kolkata's.

The case is separate from the Trinamool's internal split, in which rival camps have gone to the Election Commission over the party's name and symbol.

## What happens next

If the Supreme Court lists the state's petition, the caveat means Mr Banerjee and the Trinamool must be given notice and heard. The court could lift or modify the High Court's bar, which would allow the State Election Commission to announce the poll, or leave it in place until the High Court decides the main petition.
